A solo battleships game where learners answer future tense questions to fire at a hidden fleet on a 6×6 grid.

A solo battleships game where learners answer future tense grammar questions to fire at a hidden fleet on a 6×6 grid. Twenty questions across five categories — will/won't, going to, present continuous for future, first conditional, and timetables — with a bilingual English/French toggle throughout.

## Why it works for adult learners

The future tenses are one of the trickiest areas for French-speaking learners because French uses a single future tense where English has several overlapping forms. This game forces learners to choose between will, going to, and present continuous by reading context clues carefully — exactly the skill they need in real communication. The battleships mechanic keeps motivation high without adding cognitive noise.

## Lesson ideas

- **Pre-teaching consolidation** after introducing will vs going to vs present continuous
- **Revision warm-up** before a unit test on future forms
- **Self-study homework** — learners play solo and screenshot their final score
- **Projected whole-class version** — the teacher clicks, the class votes on the answer

## Variations

- **Team battle**: two teams alternate turns, each answering a question before choosing a cell
- **Speed round**: set a 15-second timer per question for advanced groups
- **Explain your choice**: after answering, the learner must explain why they chose that form — reinforces the grammar rule beyond just pattern-matching

Classic hexagonal grid game with intermediate business English questions — corporate vocabulary and advanced grammar structures.

Split the class into two teams. Team 1 connects top to bottom, Team 2 connects left to right. Teams take turns choosing a hexagon and answering the question to claim it. First team to complete an unbroken path wins.

A classroom take on the iconic British game show *Blockbusters*. Two teams race across a 5×5 hexagonal grid, answering intermediate business English questions to claim hexagons and build a connected path.

## What's covered

Twenty-five questions mixing **corporate vocabulary** (acquisition, merger, outsourcing, stakeholders, KPIs, USP, venture capital, downsizing) with **advanced grammar structures** (third conditional, future passive, inversion, reporting verbs, gerunds vs infinitives, subjunctive after *it's high time*).

## How to play

- Split the class into two teams of roughly equal ability.
- Team 1 tries to connect the **top to the bottom** of the board.
- Team 2 tries to connect the **left to the right**.
- Teams take turns choosing any hexagon. Read out the question — if the team answers correctly, they claim that hex in their colour.
- Both teams need a minimum path of 5 connected hexagons to win.
- Tap a team name above the board to switch turns manually if needed.

## Teaching tips

- Use this as a review activity after covering several grammar points — it works well at the end of a module.
- For grammar questions, ask the team to explain *why* their answer is correct before awarding the hex.
- Vocabulary answers often have synonyms or variants — accept any reasonable corporate equivalent.
- The strategic element (blocking the other team) is part of the fun — encourage teams to think about which hex helps their path most.
- If discussion gets too long on a hex, set a 30-second time limit per question.

Answer past simple grammar questions to fire at a hidden fleet. Sink all four ships before you run out of shots.

Tap a cell on the 6×6 grid. A past simple question appears — answer correctly to fire your shot. If there's a ship underneath, it's a hit. Sink all four ships before running out of questions. Use the language toggle to switch between English and French explanations.

## How it works

Four ships are hidden on a 6×6 grid: a Battleship (4 cells), a Cruiser (3), a Destroyer (2), and a Patrol Boat (1). Tap any cell to fire — but first you must answer a past simple question correctly. Get it wrong and you waste your shot.

You have 20 questions total, so accuracy matters. A fleet tracker shows which ships are damaged and which are sunk.

## Grammar categories

- **Regular verbs** — forming the past with *-ed*
- **Irregular verbs** — *go/went*, *buy/bought*, *write/wrote*, *drink/drank*
- **Negatives** — *didn't* + base form
- **Questions** — *Did* + subject + base form
- **Time expressions** — *yesterday*, *last week*, *ago*, *in 2019*

## Features

- 🇫🇷/🇬🇧 **bilingual toggle** — switch all questions and explanations between English and French
- **Fleet damage tracker** — visual display of each ship's status
- **Tiered end-of-game verdicts** — Cadet, Lieutenant, Captain, or Admiral depending on accuracy
- **Answer review** — review every question after the game

## Variations

- For stronger groups, set a time limit per question (use a phone timer)
- For weaker groups, allow discussion in pairs before answering
- Play as a class — project on the board, teams take turns choosing cells

- **Confidence builder** before a presentation skills lesson

- **Whole-class version**: one student at the front, the rest of the class guesses
- **Written variation**: students work in pairs to write their own taboo cards using vocabulary from a recent unit

A 5×5 Jeopardy board built around 25 high-frequency phrasal verbs at B1/B2 level. Each clue has a clear definition, the answer in capitals, and a real-world example sentence to anchor the meaning.

## Categories

- **Work & Business** — carry out, put off, hand in, come up with, look into
- **Relationships** — break up, get along, run into, stand by, look up to
- **Travel & Movement** — take off, check in, drop by, turn up, move on
- **Daily Life** — get up, try on, come across, give up, tidy up
- **Emotions** — cheer up, blow up, get over, look forward to, bottle up

## Why these phrasal verbs

These are the phrasal verbs French learners genuinely encounter — in films, in workplaces, in everyday conversation. The list deliberately mixes separable and inseparable verbs and includes a few three-word phrasal verbs (look up to, look forward to, come up with) at the higher values, since these are the ones intermediate learners typically avoid in production.

## Lesson ideas

- **End-of-unit review** after a phrasal verbs lesson — gives students a chance to recycle vocabulary in a low-stakes way.
- **Warmer for an upper-intermediate group** — even if some students don't know every verb, the game format keeps everyone engaged through the discussion phase.
- **Pre-exam practice** — phrasal verbs appear regularly in BULATS, TOEIC, Cambridge B1/B2, and DELF/DALF exams.
- **Mixed-ability classes** — let stronger students choose 400 and 500 values, weaker students 100 and 200.

## Variations

- **Sentence variation**: after a team gets the answer right, they earn double points if they can also produce a new sentence using the phrasal verb.
- **No reveals**: hide the example and ask students to make up their own sentence as part of the answer.
- **Wager round**: at the end of the game, allow each team to wager up to half their score on a final bonus phrasal verb of your choice.

## Skills covered

Listening, reading, vocabulary recall, contextual inference, paraphrasing under pressure.

Two players compete to pronounce tricky English words across three difficulty levels. IPA transcriptions and teaching notes settle every dispute.

Show the word to both players. They each attempt to say it aloud, then tap 'Reveal Pronunciation' to see the IPA and a teaching note explaining the trap. Award the point to whoever got closest — or 'Both' or 'Neither' if needed.

## How it works

A word appears on screen. Both players try to pronounce it. Tap **Reveal Pronunciation** to show the IPA transcription and a short note explaining why the word is tricky. Then award the point.

## Difficulty levels

- **Medium** — silent letters, disappearing syllables, stress traps (*comfortable*, *Wednesday*, *iron*, *receipt*…)
- **Hard** — misleading spellings, consonant clusters, stress shifts (*colonel*, *eighth*, *architecture*, *thoroughly*…)

Every word targets a specific sound or pattern that causes problems for French-speaking learners: silent consonants, unexpected vowel reductions, consonant clusters that don't exist in French, and words borrowed from French but pronounced completely differently in English.

## Variations

- Use **Medium** only for A2/B1 groups
- Use **Evil** as a fun warm-up challenge for strong B2/C1 groups
- Set it up as a team game — each team nominates a speaker per round

Why your students freeze in real meetings (and what to do about it)
Students who know vocabulary perfectly on worksheets often freeze when they need the word under pressure. Here's what's actually going on — and one classroom format that fixes it fast.

Last week I was teaching a session at a manufacturing client outside Chambéry. I asked one of the engineers — a clearly competent B2 speaker — to describe a stakeholder he was struggling with. He paused, then said: *"He is... the person who... in the project..."* and trailed off.

He knew the word "stakeholder." I'd taught it to him two months earlier. He'd used it correctly on a written exercise that same morning.

But in the moment, when he needed to *deploy* it in conversation, it wouldn't come.

This isn't a rare event. If you teach Business English, you've seen it dozens of times. And it's not a vocabulary problem. It's a retrieval problem — and most vocabulary training doesn't touch it.

## Recognition vs. retrieval

There's a meaningful difference between *knowing* a word and *being able to access* it under pressure. Cognitive scientists call this the difference between recognition and recall — and they're not the same skill.

When your student does a gap-fill exercise, they're doing recognition. The word is on the page, the context is right there, and they just have to match. Easy.

When they're in a real meeting and need to talk about a difficult stakeholder, they're doing retrieval. The context isn't laid out for them. They have to find the word, decide if it fits, and produce it — all in the time it takes for the silence to become awkward.

Most ESL textbooks build recognition. Real meetings demand retrieval. The gap between the two is where students freeze.

## What actually builds retrieval

A few things help — but they all share one feature. They force students to access vocabulary *without* being given the target word as a prompt.

**Picture descriptions** work. Show a complex image and ask students to describe what's happening — no scaffolding, no vocabulary list. They reach for the words they have.

**Role-plays with no script** work, especially if you don't pre-teach the vocabulary. The discomfort is the point.

**Taboo** works particularly well. Students have to describe a word *without* using the obvious synonyms — which means they have to access the word from multiple angles. It's retrieval under constraint, and constraint is what fluency actually is.

## Why Taboo deserves a place in every Business English lesson

I built [a free Taboo game on business meeting vocabulary](/games) — eighteen cards, sixty-second timer, no prep. I use it as a warm-up before presentation skills lessons, and I've found it does something none of my other warm-ups do.

It surfaces the gap.

When a student knows "negotiate" but can't talk around it without saying "deal" or "agreement," that's diagnostic. You've just identified exactly what to work on. The Taboo format makes the freeze moment visible — and once it's visible, you can do something about it.

The other thing it does: it builds confidence in workarounds. Real fluency isn't always knowing the perfect word. It's knowing what to do when the perfect word doesn't arrive. Students who can paraphrase, redirect, and find alternative routes through an idea are the ones who handle real meetings well.

## One practical adjustment for your next lesson

Try this: take the vocabulary you'd normally teach as a list, and present it as a Taboo deck instead. Students describe each target word to their partner *without* using the most obvious related terms.

You'll cover the same vocabulary. But instead of building recognition, you'll be building retrieval. The same words, but the right kind of practice.

The freeze moments will still happen. They'll just happen in your classroom, where you can do something about them — instead of in front of a client.

Last week I was teaching a session at a manufacturing client outside Chambéry. I asked one of the engineers — a clearly competent B2 speaker — to describe a stakeholder he was struggling with. He paused, then said: “He is… the person who… in the project…” and trailed off.

He knew the word “stakeholder.” I’d taught it to him two months earlier. He’d used it correctly on a written exercise that same morning.

But in the moment, when he needed to deploy it in conversation, it wouldn’t come.

This isn’t a rare event. If you teach Business English, you’ve seen it dozens of times. And it’s not a vocabulary problem. It’s a retrieval problem — and most vocabulary training doesn’t touch it.

Recognition vs. retrieval

There’s a meaningful difference between knowing a word and being able to access it under pressure. Cognitive scientists call this the difference between recognition and recall — and they’re not the same skill.

When your student does a gap-fill exercise, they’re doing recognition. The word is on the page, the context is right there, and they just have to match. Easy.

When they’re in a real meeting and need to talk about a difficult stakeholder, they’re doing retrieval. The context isn’t laid out for them. They have to find the word, decide if it fits, and produce it — all in the time it takes for the silence to become awkward.

Most ESL textbooks build recognition. Real meetings demand retrieval. The gap between the two is where students freeze.

What actually builds retrieval

A few things help — but they all share one feature. They force students to access vocabulary without being given the target word as a prompt.

Picture descriptions work. Show a complex image and ask students to describe what’s happening — no scaffolding, no vocabulary list. They reach for the words they have.

Role-plays with no script work, especially if you don’t pre-teach the vocabulary. The discomfort is the point.

Taboo works particularly well. Students have to describe a word without using the obvious synonyms — which means they have to access the word from multiple angles. It’s retrieval under constraint, and constraint is what fluency actually is.

Why Taboo deserves a place in every Business English lesson

I built a free Taboo game on business meeting vocabulary — eighteen cards, sixty-second timer, no prep. I use it as a warm-up before presentation skills lessons, and I’ve found it does something none of my other warm-ups do.

It surfaces the gap.

When a student knows “negotiate” but can’t talk around it without saying “deal” or “agreement,” that’s diagnostic. You’ve just identified exactly what to work on. The Taboo format makes the freeze moment visible — and once it’s visible, you can do something about it.

The other thing it does: it builds confidence in workarounds. Real fluency isn’t always knowing the perfect word. It’s knowing what to do when the perfect word doesn’t arrive. Students who can paraphrase, redirect, and find alternative routes through an idea are the ones who handle real meetings well.
